historical_timeline.summary: Born at Shadwell, Virginia (April 2, 1743, Old Style).
Writes of a violent headache of two days.
Kept at home for weeks by an illness described as an inveterate headache.
Death of his wife; months of grief he later called a stupor of mind.
First letter naming his periodical headache.
Dislocates his right wrist in Paris; it heals badly.
Takes office as Secretary of State in New York City.
A periodical headache begins in New York; the first week is violent.
Recovered after about six weeks; cinchona bark had failed for the first time; an opium remedy offered by a physician is no longer needed.
Writes that the headache of the past winter and spring came from the drudgery of business.
Daily headache fits in a dark room as President; last recorded attack in March and April 1808.
Summarizes his headaches and his stiff wrist in a letter about his health; later interpretations of the headaches differ.
Rheumatism, chronic diarrhea and difficulty passing urine in his last years; laudanum prescribed.
Dies at Monticello at 83; the exact cause was never determined. Over his lifetime he enslaved more than 600 people.

claims.statement: Thomas Jefferson was born at Shadwell, in what was then Goochland County, Virginia, on April 13, 1743 (April 2, 1743, in the Old Style calendar then in use).

source_links.locator: born on April 2, 1743; adjusted to April 13

claims.statement: He died at Monticello on July 4, 1826, at 83.

source_links.locator: died at Monticello at 12:50 p.m. on July 4, 1826

claims.statement: At 20, in a letter of March 20, 1764, written at Williamsburg late at night, he wrote of "a violent head ach, with which I have been afflicted these two days."
claims.clinical_interpretation: The earliest headache in his letters; anchors the long history in the modern episode.

claims.statement: In 1776 an illness kept him at home in Virginia for about six weeks longer than he intended; a correspondent wrote that his time at home had been interrupted by "an inveterate head ach."

source_links.locator: detained six weeks longer than I intended

claims.statement: His wife died on September 6, 1782, of complications after childbirth. In November 1782 he wrote that he was only "a little emerging from that stupor of mind which had rendered me as dead to the world as she was whose loss occasioned it."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented grief, recorded as history; the modern episode records him as a widower and screens his mood without assigning a diagnosis.

source_links.locator: complications of childbirth led to Martha Jefferson's death on September 6, 1782

claims.statement: In March 1784, at Annapolis as a delegate to Congress, he wrote that he had "lately added an attack of my periodical headach" to his habitual ill health and had to avoid reading, writing and almost thinking; his letters thereafter call the attacks his "periodical head-ach."
claims.clinical_interpretation: The term he used for the recurring headaches; the anchor of the modern presenting problem.

source_links.locator: first time Jefferson wrote the words periodical headach

claims.statement: In September 1786, in Paris, he dislocated his right wrist in a fall; the bones were set, but not well. He wrote with his left hand for a time, and in December 1788 wrote that the joint "had never been replaced," that he had lost the use of the hand "except that I can write," and that "a withered hand and swelled and crooked fingers" remained.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the synthetic stiff right wrist and the slow, painful writing in the modern episode.

source_links.locator: Wrist Injury (1786): dislocated his right wrist; 1788 December 16 letter

claims.statement: After five years in France as a diplomat, he took office as the first Secretary of State in New York City on March 21, 1790.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the setting, work and timing of the modern episode.

source_links.locator: arrived in New York City on March 21, 1790
assumed office in New York on March 21, 1790

claims.statement: In New York, a periodical headache "came on me the 1st. of May" 1790, and the first week was violent; his account books record purchases of Peruvian bark (cinchona) on May 1 and May 3.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented attack at the index date; the modern episode begins seven days into it.

claims.statement: The 1790 attack eased after the first week but lingered: on May 23 "a lingering head-ach" still kept him from business, and on June 13 he wrote that he had been able to do business for the past ten days and that it was "the first time the bark had ever failed to remove my complaint very speedily."
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the index visit; the synthetic bout settles over the same weeks.

claims.statement: During the 1790 attack a Baltimore physician wrote to him recommending a remedy containing opium for use when the bark failed; on June 13 he replied that the letter found him "so far recovered as to have no further occasion for medecine."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the teaching point that opioids are not used for migraine; no opioid use in 1790 is documented.

source_links.locator: enclosed a prescription containing volatile ammonia and opium

claims.statement: In June 1791 he wrote that a journey had freed him "from the almost constant headach with which I had been persecuted thro the whole winter and spring," and that being clear of it while travelling proved it had been "occasioned by the drudgery of business."
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode; his own view of work stress as the cause.

claims.statement: In March 1807, as President, he described daily "fits" of periodical headache lasting from about nine or ten in the morning until dark, shortening from nine hours to five, during which he was "shut up in a dark room"; the last attack recorded in his letters was in March and April 1808.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode; shows the daytime pattern and the dark room.

claims.statement: In 1819 he wrote that "a periodical head ach has afflicted me occasionally, once perhaps in 6. or 8. years, for 2 or 3 weeks at a time, which seems now to have left me," and that "a stiff wrist, the consequence of an early dislocation, makes writing both slow and painful."
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own summary of the pattern, written after the modern episode.

claims.statement: The nature of the headaches is disputed. Biographers since about 1930 have usually called them migraine, and his principal biographer called them "probably migraine"; a 1984 review argued for tension-type headaches; a 2006 review in Headache concluded that they probably were migraines, although not all current diagnostic criteria can be met; cluster headache has also been proposed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Migraine is a later interpretation, not a diagnosis made in his lifetime; the modern migraine diagnosis is synthetic.

source_links.locator: probably were migraines, although not all of the current diagnostic criteria can be met
nervous tension or muscular contraction headaches

claims.statement: A 2008 medical biography states that he intermittently experienced anxiety, depression and insomnia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretation; not used as a diagnosis in the modern episode, which screens his mood.

source_links.locator: intermittently he experienced anxiety, depression and insomnia

claims.statement: In retirement he was increasingly troubled by rheumatism, and diarrhea troubled him through the last 25 years of his life; in 1825 he had "a difficulty of making water," which his physician attributed to an enlarged prostate obstructing the flow of urine.

source_links.locator: rheumatism; diarrhea through the last twenty-five years
difficulty of making water; prostatic hypertrophy

claims.statement: In his final years his physician prescribed laudanum, a tincture of opium, for diarrhea, and he accepted its regular use because it allowed him to resume his activities.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History after the modern episode; recorded plainly as prescribed treatment of his time.

source_links.locator: laudanum, a tincture of opium, allowed him to resume activities

claims.statement: His exact cause of death was never conclusively determined; a Monticello account suggests a combination of exhaustion from severe diarrhea, kidney infection and damage, and pneumonia.

source_links.locator: exact cause of death has never been conclusively determined

claims.statement: He enslaved more than 600 people over the course of his life; Monticello gives the number as more than 610, of whom about 400 lived in bondage at Monticello.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A documented social and historical fact about his life, recorded plainly. It has no clinical role in the modern episode, and no health fact about any enslaved person is recorded.

source_links.locator: enslaved more than 610 people throughout his life

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Recurrent disabling headache in a working statesman: a 47-year-old cabinet secretary, seven weeks into a demanding new post, comes in a week into a bout of the headaches he has had since his twenties. The episode covers a structured headache history with a red-flag screen and no neuroimaging when none is indicated, a headache diary that confirms ICHD-3 migraine without aura, disability measured with the MIDAS, acute treatment with an NSAID and a triptan and the place of gepants and lasmiditan, why opioids and butalbital are avoided, counting acute-medicine days to prevent medication overuse headache, the criteria for preventive treatment and the choice among propranolol, topiramate, amitriptyline and a CGRP monoclonal antibody under the 1785 American Headache Society consensus, its 1788 position statement and the 1789 ACP guidelines, sleep, meals, caffeine and work stress as triggers, and an old badly healed wrist injury that makes writing slow and painful.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Jefferson returns with his 14-day headache diary and is seen by Dr. Haddad of headache medicine on the same day. The bout that began three weeks ago has eased. His diary shows headache on 7 of 14 days: each attack began between nine and ten in the morning, built over an hour to a moderate or severe throbbing pain across the forehead and temples, worse with reading and climbing stairs, with sensitivity to light and noise on every headache day and nausea on four, and lasted six to ten hours, settling by evening. He had no visual or other aura. The last seven days have been headache-free. He took naproxen on four days, with metoclopramide on two, and the pain was reduced but rarely gone after two hours; he has taken no combination analgesic since intake. Counting the week before intake, he has had 13 migraine days in the past four weeks. He has been sleeping six hours, has kept to two cups of coffee and has not skipped lunch. He has had no weakness, numbness, fever or change in vision.

referral.question: Recurrent disabling headaches since his twenties, in bouts of near-daily morning-onset attacks lasting weeks, in a 47-year-old cabinet secretary now in the seventh day of a bout. Please confirm the diagnosis and advise on acute and preventive treatment
referral.urgency: Within two weeks, on the day of his two-week primary care review, with the headache diary
referral.pertinent_history: Headaches since about 20, in bouts lasting from two days to several weeks every few years, with long gaps; the current bout began a week ago in the first weeks of a demanding new post. Each attack begins mid-morning, builds to a severe throbbing pain across the forehead and temples with sensitivity to light and noise and some nausea, stops him reading or writing, and settles by evening. No aura. No thunderclap onset, fever, weight loss, neurological symptoms, positional or exertional features, or change in the pattern; neurological examination and fundi normal. He has used an over-the-counter aspirin, acetaminophen and caffeine combination on 9 days in the past month, with little effect. MIDAS 39 (grade IV), HIT-6 66, PHQ-9 6 (item 9 scored 0), GAD-7 7, AUDIT-C 3. Blood pressure 126/80, pulse 74; never smoked; no vascular disease, asthma or heart block. An old right wrist dislocation, badly healed, makes writing slow and painful. Today: the combination analgesic stopped; naproxen 500 mg with metoclopramide 10 mg as needed, no more than two days a week; a 14-day diary; no imaging
questions: Do his headaches meet ICHD-3 criteria for migraine, and is any other primary or secondary headache likely?
Is neuroimaging or any other test needed?
What acute treatment do you advise, and what should he avoid?
Is preventive treatment indicated, and which medicine fits a man whose work depends on reading and writing?
How should we prevent medication overuse headache and manage long bouts?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Jefferson, a 47-year-old cabinet secretary, is seen at the request of Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz with a 14-day headache diary. He has had headaches since about 20, coming in bouts that last from days to several weeks, every few years, often at times of heavy work. The present bout began three weeks ago. In the diary, headache came on 7 of 14 days, starting between nine and ten in the morning and lasting six to ten hours, throbbing and moderate to severe across the forehead and temples, worse with reading and climbing stairs, with light and noise sensitivity on every headache day and nausea on four. He has never had an aura. The last seven days have been free. Naproxen on four days helped partly. He stopped the combination analgesic at intake. He sleeps about six hours, drinks two cups of coffee a day and skips meals on busy days
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Beaumont-Ruiz's intake note and the 14-day diary. MIDAS 39 (grade IV) and HIT-6 66 at intake; PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 7, AUDIT-C 3. Blood pressure 122/78 and pulse 70 today. No laboratory tests or imaging have been done, and none are needed

assessment.display: Migraine without aura, episodic, with bouts of near-daily attacks
assessment.assessment: ICHD-3 criteria are met: at least five attacks of 4 to 72 hours with throbbing, moderate to severe pain worsened by routine activity, nausea, and light and noise sensitivity, not better accounted for by another diagnosis. Tension-type headache does not cause this severity, nausea or disability, though neck tension may add to it. Cluster headache does not fit: his attacks last hours, come by day, and lack one-sided eye symptoms. Medication overuse headache is not present, since the combination analgesic was used on fewer than 10 days a month and has stopped

A long, stable pattern with a normal neurological examination and no red flags does not call for brain imaging or blood tests; imaging would be considered for a new or changed pattern, a sudden severe headache, neurological signs, fever or onset after 50

Naproxen alone gives partial relief. A triptan with an NSAID taken early in the attack is the most effective first choice; he has no cardiovascular contraindication. A gepant or lasmiditan is the alternative if a triptan fails or becomes unsuitable. Opioids and butalbital should be avoided: they work poorly for migraine and raise the risk of medication overuse headache

Bouts bring 13 migraine days in four weeks with severe disability (MIDAS 39), which meets the 1785 American Headache Society criteria for offering prevention. Propranolol is well established and inexpensive, and suits his normal blood pressure and lack of asthma. Topiramate can slow word-finding and concentration, and amitriptyline can cause morning drowsiness, both poor fits for his work. The 1788 AHS position statement makes a CGRP monoclonal antibody a first-line option, while the 1789 ACP guideline places it after the first-line oral preventives; after discussing both, he chose propranolol first, with an antibody as the next step
Neck and shoulder tension from long writing with a painful wrist may add to his headaches; hand therapy, a splint and dictation are worth doing

recommendations: Sumatriptan 100 mg with naproxen 500 mg early in an attack, with a second sumatriptan after two hours if needed; no more than nine triptan days a month
Propranolol extended-release 80 mg each evening, raised to 120 mg at four weeks if pulse and blood pressure allow; judge the effect at two to three months, seeking at least half as many migraine days
A CGRP monoclonal antibody if propranolol is not tolerated or does not work
Keep acute medicine to two days a week or fewer, count the days in the diary, and avoid opioids, butalbital and combination products with caffeine
No brain imaging unless the pattern changes or red flags appear

For an attack lasting more than 72 hours, or a bout of daily attacks that the plan does not control, call the clinic for a short scheduled bridge (naproxen twice daily for up to five days) or treatment in clinic, rather than daily triptans or extra analgesics
A fixed wake time, regular meals, steady caffeine, daily walks, regular breaks from reading, and hand therapy and dictation for the wrist
